title: Say It Bar
context: Grade 4, and this is where the writing of a decimal and the meaning of it become one skill. An adult sees a number being read out loud. What is actually being taught is that the last word of the spoken sentence names a place, and that the place name says how many digits the decimal part has to have. A child who has only ever read decimals digit by digit can say a number perfectly and still write five and ninety-six thousandths with two digits after the point.

writeup.why: Cut a number where its dot is, name what each side is doing, and build the sentence that reads the whole thing aloud.
writeup.look: A number lying along a bar with its point standing between the halves, a sentence builder under it and a second reading lane below that.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Say It Bar' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the sentences finished against the sentences this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each sentence reaches its last word and the second fixed at however many this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The bar lies across the top of the working area, 1080 by 120 at 64,220, carrying one number in digit cards 84 wide, the cards to the left of the point deep blue and those to the right of it green, with the point drawn as a standing divider 16 wide and the full height of the bar, in vermilion, resting on the baseline of the digits and never floating above or below it. Cut at the point slides the two halves 40 apart along the bar and drops a label under each, the whole number part on the left and the decimal part on the right, each label read out as what its side is counting: whole ones to the left, pieces smaller than one to the right. The sentence builder stands under the bar, four slots in a row at 64,390, each 250 by 90 with 12 between them, taking in order the whole number part, the joining word, the decimal part read as though it were a whole number, and the place name of its last digit. The slots fill left to right and the place name slot refuses any name that does not match the digits standing to the right of the point: the refusal springs the name back with nothing marked, and count the places runs along those digits from the point outwards, lighting and numbering them one at a time. The everyday lane runs the same four slots again at 64,500, with the word point in the joining slot and the digits after the point shown one at a time rather than as a number. The hearing bay runs along the foot of the working area, 1080 by 110 at 64,610: a sentence arrives in it already built, the place name at its end lights first, and that many empty places are drawn to the right of a point above the bay for the child to fill from the left, with any place the heard digits do not reach left drawn open until a grey zero is put into it. Say it again reads the finished sentence back with its last word lit. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a number is asked for, and beside them the place name tray, three keys reading tenths, hundredths and thousandths, with the joining keys and the word point under them, so that a whole sentence can be built by press as well as by drag. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a digit standing to the left of the point is deep blue, a digit standing to the right of it is green, and the point itself is vermilion between them on every phase without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is one dot cannot afford a frame where the dot has to be hunted for. A part standing for tenths is amber, one standing for hundredths is rose, one standing for thousandths is sky blue, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey, whether it was written in on the left of a short numerator or printed on the end of a measurement. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every one of the readings survives with the colour taken away, because a place is told by the heading written over it before it is ever told by a colour, a filling zero is told by the short arrow running inward from the point, and a zero printed on the end is told by the place counter that lights it. Grey never means faint: such a zero is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. The two readings are never drawn mixed. A lane carries either the word and with its decimal part read as one number, or the word point with its digits read singly, and a slot filled from the other lane's tray springs back with both lanes left standing, because half of one reading and half of the other is the sentence that hides which place the last digit is in.
writeup.finish: The card shows the number the child read, cut at its point with both halves named, and the sentence they built standing under it.

phases.win: both labels land, the left half lit as whole ones and the right half as pieces smaller than one
phases.does: cuts the bar at the point and drops a label on each half
phases.goal: the two parts of a decimal are named and each is doing its own job
phases.says: Cut it where the dot is. What is each side counting?
phases.check: Away from the screen: write a decimal of your own and draw a line through its point. Say what each side counts.
phases.feels: one dot, and everything on one side of it is whole things while everything on the other side is pieces
phases.hands: Write a decimal large on the board and draw a vertical line straight down through its point. Ask what the digits on the left are counting and what the digits on the right are counting, and write those two answers under the two halves rather than saying them. Then cover one half at a time with a sheet of paper and ask what is left standing each time.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: where is the dot in this number? Second rung, the phase's: which side of it counts whole ones? Third rung: the bar is cut to one digit either side and the child drops both labels. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: every number read aloud before this chapter was one run of digits, and the dot is the smallest mark on the line.
wrong.move: reads the whole thing straight through as one long number and loses the dot somewhere in the middle.
wrong.screen: the bar cuts itself at the point and the two halves slide apart along the bar with the standing divider left between them, and each half is read out on its own with its label dropping under it. The number the child said stays written in the slot, and a card carrying that number with no point in it at all is laid under the bar so the two can be read against each other.

wrong.why: the digits on the right look exactly like the digits on the left and nothing about their shape says they are counting something smaller.
wrong.move: labels the right hand half as though its digits counted whole ones too, so a decimal part of three digits is read as hundreds.
wrong.screen: the right hand half is carried down to the grid and the strip, where its digits are laid out as pieces smaller than one and take up less than a single whole between them. The child's label stays exactly where it was dropped, the whole number part is drawn out beside it in whole ones, and the two sit on the stage together at their real sizes.

phases.screen: a number lying along the bar with the point standing between its halves
phases.soWhat: A decimal has two parts separated by the point, the whole number part on the left and the decimal part on the right.
phases.concept: The point divides the number in two

phases.win: both lanes read the same number, one with the word and, one with the word point
phases.does: drops the joining word in, then runs the everyday lane and compares the two
phases.goal: the point is read as the word and, with the everyday reading allowed beside it
phases.says: What word goes where the dot is? Now try the everyday way.
phases.check: Read a decimal of your own aloud in both ways, and say which word took the place of the dot each time.
phases.feels: two readings, both of them allowed, and each one has to be said all the way through
phases.hands: Read a decimal aloud twice, once with the word and and the decimal part said as one number, and once with the word point and the digits said one at a time. Have the class write down which reading they heard each time. Then read a third one badly on purpose, mixing the two, and ask what went wrong and what the number could now be.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which word is standing in the joining slot? Second rung, the phase's: which reading does that word belong to? Third rung: the bar is cut to one digit after the point and the child runs both lanes on it. The joining keys stay open.

wrong.why: prices are read that way out loud all the time, and each half of the mixture is a piece of a reading the chapter has actually taught.
wrong.move: says the word point and then reads the decimal part as one whole number, mixing the two readings into one.
wrong.screen: both lanes run the number as it stands, the upper with the word and and the decimal part as one number, the lower with the word point and the digits singly, and the child's reading is written on a third line under them exactly as it was said. The place name that each proper reading ends on is lit, and the mixed line is left with nothing lit at its end.

wrong.why: the word and is used that way in ordinary speech about whole numbers, and it has just been handed over as the word for the point.
wrong.move: puts the word and in the middle of the whole number part as well, so the joining word turns up twice in one sentence.
wrong.screen: the sentence is read back with each slot lighting as it is spoken, and the joining slot lights alone on the word and while the whole number part is read out of a single slot. The child's sentence stays standing underneath, with both of its ands drawn in, and the point on the bar is lit against the one that is doing that job.

phases.screen: the sentence builder with the joining slot empty between the two parts
phases.soWhat: The word and stands for the point in the proper reading, and the word point stands for it in the everyday one.

phases.win: the place name lands and the counted digits light from the point outwards to match it
phases.does: counts the digits after the point, then chooses the place name for the last one
phases.goal: the last word of the sentence names the place the last digit sits in
phases.says: Count what is after the dot. Which place does the last one sit in?
phases.check: Read a number with three digits after the point aloud. Which word does the reading end on, and which digit chose it?
phases.feels: the sentence ends on the place of the last digit, and the count that finds it starts at the dot
phases.hands: Read a number with three digits after the point aloud, slowly, and stop hard on the last word. Ask what would change if one digit were rubbed off the end, and let the class hear the last word change with it. Then write four numbers on cards with different numbers of places and have them sorted by the word their reading ends on.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many digits are after the dot? Second rung, the phase's: which of them is the last one? Third rung: the number is cut to two digits after the point and the child counts and names. The place name tray stays open.

wrong.why: the first digit after the point is the one the eye reaches first and the tenths place is the one named earliest in the chapter.
wrong.move: names the place of the FIRST digit after the point and ends the sentence on tenths.
wrong.screen: count the places runs from the point outwards with each digit lighting and being numbered as it is passed, and the count holds on the last digit at the far end. The child's name stays in the slot, the name the count calls for is offered from the tray beside it, and both names are left standing under the same number.

wrong.why: a number is read from the left and counting from the left is how every count so far has gone, and on a number with one digit in front of the point the two counts can land on the same digit.
wrong.move: counts the places from the left hand end of the whole number, so the count starts before the point.
wrong.screen: the place chart slides in behind the number with the point column drawn in it, and the counting is run twice: once from the left hand end of the number, which stops in the whole number part, and once from the point outwards. Both runs stay drawn with their counts written above the digits, and the number is then given two digits in front of the point instead of one, where the two runs plainly part.

phases.screen: the sentence built as far as the decimal part, with the place name slot waiting
phases.soWhat: The last word of the sentence names the place the last digit sits in.

phases.win: every place is filled, with a zero taking the place the digits heard did not reach
phases.does: reads the place name, lays out the empty places, then fills them from the left
phases.goal: the place name says how many digits the decimal part needs
phases.says: The last word tells you how many places. Fill them in from the left.
phases.check: Write forty-one and six hundredths as a decimal, and say how many places the last word asked for.
phases.feels: the last word settles how many places there are before there is a single digit to put in them
phases.hands: One child reads a card aloud using the place name at the end while the rest write what they hear on small boards. Compare the boards before the card is shown. Ask where the boards disagreed and whether the trouble was the reading or the number of digits after the point. Then say an amount whose digits do not fill the places the last word calls for, and let them find the gap.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the last word of the sentence? Second rung, the phase's: how many places does that word ask for? Third rung: the bay is cut to an amount ending in tenths and the child lays out the places before writing anything. The number pad and the place name tray stay open.

wrong.why: eighty-five is two digits and there are two digits to write, so the number seems to have filled the places it was given.
wrong.move: writes seven and eighty-five thousandths with two places after the point, giving seven point eight five.
wrong.screen: the last word of the heard sentence lights and three empty places are drawn to the right of the point, and the child's two digits are walked into the two places furthest from the point, leaving the place nearest the point drawn open. The child's number stays written underneath, and the number the places call for is read back with its last digit in the thousandths place.

wrong.why: a place is empty and a zero is a spare digit, so it seems to belong wherever there is room for it, and the right hand end is where a digit usually gets added.
wrong.move: fills the third place by hanging a zero on the right hand end of the eighty-five instead of on its left.
wrong.screen: both numbers are built out to three places and read back by their last digits, the child's ending in the thousandths place with an eight standing in the tenths, and the proper one with the eight in the hundredths. A short arrow is drawn running inward from the point to the place that was actually empty, which is the one nearest the point and on the LEFT of the digits, and the two numbers stand together with the grey zero walked across into that place.

phases.screen: a spoken sentence in the hearing bay with its last word lit and the places drawn empty
phases.soWhat: The place name at the end says how many digits the decimal part must have.
phases.concept: Writing one down from what you hear

writeup.delight: The third phase, when the place name lands. The name settles into the last slot and the digits to the right of the point light back the other way, one at a time from the point outwards, with the count drawn over each as it lights, and the last of them holds lit under the name that has just been chosen. Pull a digit off the end of the number and the whole thing runs again on its own: the count is one shorter, the name in the slot lifts out and the tray offers the name that now fits. The sentence can be lengthened and shortened as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a number lies along the bar in one piece with the point standing between its halves and two blank labels lying on the ledge below it. On the second the bar is already cut and labelled and the sentence builder stands under it with the joining slot empty between the two parts. On the third the sentence is built as far as the decimal part and only the place name slot is waiting, with the digits after the point drawn and uncounted. On the fourth the upper lane is empty and a sentence already built lies in the hearing bay with its last word lit and a row of empty places drawn to the right of a point. The running count at the top left holds the sentences finished against the sentences this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the standing point, or the empty joining slot, or the last digit after the point, or the lit last word of the heard sentence, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what each side of the dot is counting. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number on the bar, either lane, with the hearing bay open and the place name tray loaded. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on naming the two parts, saying the point, naming the last digit's place, and writing a decimal down from the words that were heard.
voiceLines: A number along a bar, with a dot standing in the middle of it. Cut it there.
Cut it where the dot is. What is each side counting?
What word goes where the dot is? Now try the everyday way.
Count what is after the dot. Which place does the last one sit in?
The last word tells you how many places. Fill them in from the left.
Another number. Read the whole part first and say the dot after it.
Free play. Any number on the bar, either lane, with the hearing bay open.
Count the digits after the dot again, and leave the last word until last.
Every sentence built to its last word, and every last word doing a job.

observations.why: The last word names the place of the last digit, so it is fixed by how many digits there are.
observations.soWhat: The last word of the sentence is not a decoration; it is the word that says how long the decimal part is.
observations.observe: The place name slot would not take a name that did not match the digits counted after the point.

observations.why: One reading uses the word and with the decimal part read as a whole number, and the other uses the word point with the digits read singly.
observations.soWhat: Both readings are allowed, and each one has to be said whole rather than half and half.
observations.observe: Both lanes read the same number and neither of them was the correct one.

observations.why: The place name settles how many places there are before there is anything to put in them.
observations.soWhat: Writing a decimal down from words starts with the number of places, not with the digits.
observations.observe: The heard sentence gave its last word first and its digits second, which is the opposite of the writing order.

observations.why: The sentence had already said how many places there were, so the place existed before anything filled it.
observations.soWhat: A short decimal part is filled out with a zero on the left of the digits, between them and the point.
observations.observe: A place the heard digits did not reach stayed drawn and open until a zero went into it.

source_tool.description: A number lies along a bar across the stage with its point drawn as a standing divider between the two halves. A cutting control separates the bar at the point and drops a label on each half, naming the whole number part on the left and the decimal part on the right. Under the bar a sentence builder waits with four slots in a row: the whole number part, the joining word, the decimal part read as though it were a whole number, and the place name of its last digit. The slots fill in that order, and the place name slot refuses any name that does not match the number of digits standing to the right of the point, which are counted and lit from the point outwards as the child reaches for it. A second lane under the first runs the everyday reading beside it, with the word point in the joining slot and the digits after the point shown one at a time. A hearing bay runs the job backwards: a sentence arrives already built, the place name at its end is lit first, and that many empty places are drawn to the right of a point for the child to fill from the left, with any place the heard digits do not reach left visibly open until a zero is put in it.
source_tool.art_direction: A number on a bar, sentence beneath / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a strip that can be cut, a ten by ten grid whose cells can be tapped, digit cards that can be picked up, a point card of its own, a ruled place chart with a heading over every column, a kitchen scale with a printing display, and a balance beam.

A whole is always drawn split into parts of the same size, with the parts touching so that the whole is still one thing. Exactly the stated number of parts is drawn, exactly the stated number of them is shaded, and no part overlaps another.

A decimal is always drawn with its point standing clearly between the two parts and never floating above or below the line. Where the two parts are named, the whole number part is named on the left and the decimal part on the right.

A place chart always carries a named heading over every column, holds one digit to a column, and keeps a column of its own for the dot between the ones and the tenths. A bare row of digits with no chart behind it is never used to teach place value.

A zero filling an empty decimal place is drawn arriving from the point outwards, on the left of the digits already there, with a short arrow running inward from the point. That arrow never runs the other way.

A zero printed on the end of a decimal is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit, and it is never dimmed, shrunk, tidied away or quietly dropped. The whole teaching of the closing topic is that it counts.

Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one above the other, with whatever measures the difference between them drawn in between. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
A column, a place or a part is told apart by its label first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a part or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. A digit to the left of the point is deep blue and a digit to the right of it is green, with the decimal point itself vermilion between them in every tool without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is one dot cannot afford a frame where the dot has to be hunted for. A part standing for tenths is amber, one standing for hundredths is rose and one standing for thousandths is sky blue, and those three hold from the strip to the grid to the chart. A zero holding a place open is grey, whether it was filled in on the left of a short numerator or printed on the end of a measurement, because it is the one digit here doing a job rather than counting something. Grey never means faint: such a zero is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. All of that holds in greyscale, because a filling zero is told apart by the short arrow running inward from the point, and a printed zero on the end by the place counter that lights it.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.

voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.

voice.onNext: Another number. Read the whole part first and say the dot after it.
voice.opening: A number along a bar, with a dot standing in the middle of it. Cut it there.
voice.onFinish: Every sentence built to its last word, and every last word doing a job.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any number on the bar, either lane, with the hearing bay open.

phase_map.concept: The point divides the number in two
Writing one down from what you hear

placement.where: After a decimal has been read aloud badly once, digit by digit, with the place name left off the end. The tool is what holds the whole sentence on the stage while it is being built, so the last word is seen to be doing a job rather than tacked on.

answer_key.rule: A decimal has two parts separated by the point. The whole number part is on the left and counts whole ones; the decimal part is on the right and counts pieces smaller than one. To read one properly, read the whole number part as usual, say the word and for the point, read the decimal part as though it were a whole number, and then name the place the LAST digit sits in. The everyday reading says point instead of and and reads the digits after the point one at a time, and both readings are allowed. Writing one down from words runs the same rule backwards: the place name at the end says how many digits the decimal part must have, and a number too short for them is filled out with a zero in front of it.
answer_key.wrong: The bar is cut again at the point, the digits on the right are counted and lit one at a time, and the sentence is rebuilt slot by slot with the place name left until last. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The point separates the number into two parts, and everything to its left is the whole number part.
So 45 is the whole number part, and those digits count whole ones.
Everything to the right of the point is the decimal part, so 317 is the decimal part, counting pieces smaller than one.
items.answer: 45 is the whole number part and 317 is the decimal part
items.question: In 45.317, which digits make the whole number part and which make the decimal part?
items.checkpoint: The point marks where the whole ones stop and the pieces smaller than one start.
items.misconception: Reading the whole thing as one long number and losing the point somewhere in the middle of it.

steps: The whole number part is eight, and it is read just as it always was.
The word and takes the place of the point, and the decimal part is read as the whole number sixty-four.
Two digits sit after the point, so the last one is in the hundredths place, giving eight and sixty-four hundredths; the everyday reading is eight point six four.
items.answer: Eight and sixty-four hundredths, or eight point six four
items.question: Read 8.64 aloud in the proper way, and then in the everyday way.
items.checkpoint: The word and stands for the point in the proper reading, and the word point stands for it in the everyday one.
items.misconception: Saying eight point sixty-four, which mixes the two readings and hides which place the four is in.

steps: Fifty-six is the whole number part, and the word and takes the place of the point.
The decimal part is read as though it were the whole number two hundred four.
Three digits sit after the point, so the last one is in the thousandths place, and the reading ends on the word thousandths.
items.answer: Fifty-six and two hundred four thousandths
items.question: Read 56.204 aloud in the proper way.
items.checkpoint: The place name at the end is the place of the LAST digit, not of the first one.
items.misconception: Ending on tenths, because the first digit after the point is the one in the tenths place.

steps: Seven is the whole number part, so it goes to the left of the point.
The last word is thousandths, so three places are needed to the right of the point.
Eighty-five fills only two of them, so a zero goes in front of it in the tenths place, giving 7.085.
items.question: Write seven and eighty-five thousandths as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: The place name at the end says how many digits the decimal part must have.
items.misconception: Writing 7.85, which has two places and reads as seven and eighty-five hundredths.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: In 13.9, name the whole number part and name the decimal part.
items.final_answer: 13 is the whole number part and 9 is the decimal part

items.question: Which part of a decimal counts pieces smaller than one?
items.final_answer: The decimal part, which is written to the right of the point

items.question: Read 2.7 aloud in the everyday way.
Which word takes the place of the point when a decimal is read in the proper way?
Read 30.45 aloud in the proper way.
Read 0.608 aloud in the proper way.
Write forty-one and six hundredths as a decimal.
A rate is read out as twenty-six and forty-five hundredths rupees. Write it as a decimal, and say how many decimal places it needs.
items.final_answer: 26.45, and it needs two decimal places

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: separates the bar into its two parts and labels each one
takes the whole number part, the joining word, the decimal part and the place name in order
counts and lights the digits standing to the right of the point
offers tenths, hundredths and thousandths for the last slot
runs the second reading, with point in the joining slot and the digits read singly
hands over a spoken sentence and takes the number written from it
shows the places still waiting when the digits heard do not fill them
reads the finished sentence back with its last word lit

teaching_notes: The chapter reads 32.198 out in full as thirty-two and one hundred ninety-eight thousandths, and then writes seventeen and three tenths back as 17.3. Those two together are the whole topic: one job run in each direction. Read the first one aloud before the tool is opened, slowly, and stop hard on the last word. Ask what would change if there were only two digits after the point, and let the class hear the last word change with it. Insist that the two readings are never mixed. Eight point sixty-four is the reading that hides the place, and it is the one that comes out of a class that has only ever read prices aloud. Both readings are allowed, but each one has to be said whole. Running the rule backwards is where the work is, so spend the time there. The place name is heard first and the digits second, which is the opposite of the order they get written in, and the empty places control is what keeps the gap visible while the digits are being laid in. A packet out of a kitchen cupboard is worth bringing in for the last of it. Every nutrition panel on one is decimals, read aloud by somebody every day with the place names left off, and asking for five of them written down is the quickest way to find out whether the reading has stuck.
generation_prompt: Build a reading tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A decimal lies along a horizontal bar across the working area with its point drawn as a standing divider between the two halves. A cut control separates the bar at the point and drops a label on each half, naming the whole number part on the left and the decimal part on the right. Under the bar sits a sentence builder with four slots in a row: the whole number part, the joining word, the decimal part read as a whole number, and the place name of its last digit. The slots fill left to right, and the place name slot refuses any name that does not match the number of digits standing to the right of the point, which are counted and lit from the point outwards as the child reaches for it, with nothing marked. A second lane under the first runs the everyday reading, with the word point in the joining slot and the digits after the point shown one at a time. A hearing bay hands over a sentence already built, lights the place name at its end first, and draws that many empty places waiting to the right of a point for the child to fill from the left; a place the heard digits do not reach stays visibly open until a zero is put into it. A say it again control reads the finished sentence back with its last word lit. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Cut the number where the dot is. Name the part on each side. Read the whole number part first. Say and for the dot. Then count the digits after the dot and name the place the last one sits in.
